title: Expat Life in Cambodia Without a Bank Account: Small Riel Notes, KHQR, and the Day the Math Stops
summary: How expats in Cambodia handle rent-adjacent life, markets, tuk-tuks, and the USD-riel shuffle without a local bank account, using KHQR codes and a wallet funded from home.
body_markdown:
It is 7:40 in the morning at a coffee cart off Street 240 in Phnom Penh. The iced coffee costs a dollar fifty. You hand over two US dollars, and the woman behind the cart hands you back a 2,000 riel note, because nobody gives coins here and fifty cents of change always comes back in riel. You now have one more small purple note to add to the fold of them in your pocket, the ones you keep meaning to spend and never quite do. The man in front of you did none of this. He held his phone up to a laminated square on the counter, tapped once, and walked off with his coffee. That square was a[KHQR](https://moretapay.com/networks/khqr) code, and it is quietly the answer to half the money questions expats ask when they move here.


## Two Currencies, One Wallet, Constant Arithmetic


Cambodia runs on two currencies at once. US dollars handle the bigger numbers: rent deposits, a nice dinner, a monthly gym pass. Riel handles everything small, and critically, it handles change. Pay for a $2.75 lunch with a five, and your change arrives as a mix of dollar bills and riel notes converted at the rounded conventional rate everyone silently agrees on. It works, locals do it without thinking, but for a newcomer it means every single cash transaction involves a small mental conversion, a quick check of the notes you were handed, and a growing stack of low-value riel that is awkward to spend anywhere except the exact kind of small purchase you were trying to simplify in the first place.


Add the classic cash problems on top. Torn or worn dollar bills get refused. Large bills get the pained look and the "no change, sorry" at small stalls. And if you are living here rather than visiting for a week, you are doing this dance every day, several times a day.


## Bakong and KHQR: The System Locals Already Switched To


Over the past few years, Cambodia's central bank built a national payment backbone called Bakong, and with it a standard QR format called KHQR. The result is that one style of QR code now sits on counters everywhere: the pharmacy, the phone shop, the vegetable seller at Boeung Keng Kang market, the tuk-tuk driver who printed his code and zip-tied it to the back of the passenger seat. Khmer customers scan it with their local banking apps, the money lands instantly, and nobody counts change.


KHQR also neatly sidesteps the dual-currency confusion. The merchant's code specifies what they charge, you see the exact amount before confirming, and there is no change to calculate because there is no change at all. The riel-versus-dollar question becomes the app's problem, not a negotiation at the counter.


The catch for expats has always been access. Those local banking apps generally want a Cambodian bank account, which usually means a visa with the right duration, paperwork, and a branch visit or two. Plenty of long-term expats eventually do it. But plenty of others, especially in their first months, or on visa situations that make account opening annoying, live here for a long time without one.


## How Expats Actually Cope Without a Local Account


Talk to expats in Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, or Kampot and you hear the same workarounds. Some run everything through ATM withdrawals from their home bank, eating the fees and rationing crisp bills. Some find a friend with a local account and settle up in cash, which works until the friend leaves. Some keep a strict envelope system: dollars in one pocket, riel in the other, and a prayer that today's bills pass the tear inspection.


All of these work, sort of. None of them get you into the KHQR ecosystem, which is where daily life actually happens now. And that is the real gap: it is not that you cannot pay in Cambodia without a bank account, it is that you are stuck in the cash lane while everyone around you moved to the fast one.

## A Realistic Split: Where You Still Want Cash


Honesty matters here, because Cambodia is not fully cashless and will not be soon. Keep some small riel for the handful of situations QR has not reached: a remote countryside stall, an older vendor who never printed a code, a temple donation box. A few dollars in clean small bills still earn their place in your wallet. The shift is in proportion. Instead of cash being your entire system, it becomes the backup you reach for once or twice a week, while KHQR handles the daily grind.


One habit worth building early: lock your phone properly and know how to freeze your wallet remotely, since your phone is now effectively your money. We wrote a full walkthrough on


[what happens to a QR payment app if your phone gets stolen abroad](https://moretapay.com/blog/how-secure-is-a-qr-payment-app-abroad-once-your-phone-gets-stolen)


, and the short version is that a wallet you can freeze from a laptop is far safer than a pocket of unmarked bills you cannot.


## What Day One Looks Like


Set the wallet up before your flight or on your first evening: connect your home bank or card, top up in your own currency, done. The next morning, order that iced coffee, point your phone at the laminated square, check the amount and the rate on screen, and tap confirm. No change, no conversion math, no new riel note joining the pocket collection. That is the whole trick, and it is the same trick locals have been using for years.
